title: Original TEST: apply rectangle area rule to measured floor mat
subject: TEST
scope_summary: Wholly AUTHORED TEST APPLY-D1 with supplied A=length×width rule. Protected W: for a 7cm by 4cm rectangular mat apply the formula to calculate 28 square centimetres with units; Core1A distinct 3 by 5, Core1B wrong addition on 5 by 3 and fresh square 4 by 4 boundary; inverse Core2B given area 24 and width 4 infer length 6. microtopics.title: Explain the pairing mechanism behind an even total from two odd groups
microtopics.badge_reason: One causal sentence about the two leftovers, supported by a pair diagram.
entry_assumptions: An even group divides into pairs with no leftover.
An odd group divides into pairs with exactly one leftover.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Explain that the one leftover from EACH odd group combines into a new pair, so every combined counter belongs to a pair.

teaching_path.action: Describe odd groups by complete pairs plus one leftover counter, without classifying a target sum.
teaching_path.why_valid: This is the counter-pair definition of odd cardinality.
teaching_path.output: Complete pairs and one lone counter

teaching_path.action: Join a different worked set of 3 and 5 counters and place their two lone counters together.
teaching_path.why_valid: The worked groups each have one remainder, which forms a complete new pair.

teaching_path.action: Check the worked result by listing the four complete pairs and explaining why none is unpaired.
teaching_path.why_valid: Three plus five has eight counters forming four whole pairs; this illustrates the mechanism without answering the 7+9 task.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Odd plus odd must be odd because both starting groups are odd.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: A student claims 5+7 is odd because each group has one lone counter. What happens to the two lone counters after joining?
misconceptions.repair: The two lone counters pair with each other. No lone counter remains; 5+7 is even.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: An even result only needs a numerical sum; no explanation of grouping is necessary.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: If you write 7+9=16, what counter structure establishes WHY sixteen is even?
misconceptions.repair: Identify three pairs plus one lone in seven, four pairs plus one lone in nine, then the lone pair. All eight final pairs are complete.

exit_task.prompt: Independent exit: explain why combining groups of 11 and 13 counters gives an even group, describing the fate of both unpaired counters (not merely computing the sum).

answer.summary: Each odd group leaves one counter; those two become another pair, so 11+13 forms 12 complete pairs, an even total.
reasoning: 11 counters form five pairs plus one lone.
13 counters form six pairs plus one lone.
The lone counters join to make the twelfth pair.
All 24 counters now belong to complete pairs; 24 is even.
answer.check: 11+13=24 and 24=2×12 validates the count after the pairing explanation.

task.prompt: A learner argues '5 plus 7 must be odd because both groups are odd'. Each odd group has complete pairs and one lone counter. Explain whether the reasoning is right and trace the two lone counters after joining. Write before opening the reconstruction.
givens: 5 is two complete pairs plus one lone.

boundary_test.prompt: Changed case: combine 9 counters (four pairs plus one) with 4 counters (two whole pairs). Explain why the result is ODD using leftovers; do not merely compute 13.
boundary_test.answer: The nine-counter group leaves one lone; the four-counter group contributes no lone. That single counter stays unpaired, so the joined group is odd.
boundary_test.confirms: Differentiates two-odd leftovers from odd-plus-even with exactly one leftover; not a memorized 5+7 explanation.

questions.stem: Worked DIFFERENT example: one group has 3 counters, another 5. Explain why joining them makes an even group by tracking complete pairs and their two leftover counters.
conditions: Counters are distinct objects; groups can be arranged into pairs.
Even means no lone counter; odd means exactly one lone counter.
The question is original AUTHORED TEST, no organizer source.

answer.summary: 3 is one pair plus one lone; 5 is two pairs plus one lone. The two lone counters pair up, leaving four pairs and an even total 8.
reasoning: Three has one pair and one lone counter.
Five has two pairs and one lone counter.
The two lone counters become a fourth pair, leaving none unpaired.
Therefore the joined set is even.

reasoning_route.why_valid: Three and five each leave one when paired.

questions.stem: An organizer places 7 red counters and 9 blue counters into ONE collection. Without relying only on the arithmetic total, EXPLAIN why the combined collection can be arranged into complete PAIRS with NO leftover counter. Name what happens to the one unmatched counter from EACH original odd group.
conditions: Counters are distinct objects; groups can be arranged into pairs.
Even means no lone counter; odd means exactly one lone counter.
The question is original AUTHORED TEST, no organizer source.

answer.summary: Seven gives three complete pairs and one lone; nine gives four pairs and one lone. The two lone counters pair together, so eight pairs contain all 16 counters, making the total even.
reasoning: Seven red counters can be grouped as three pairs and one lone.
Nine blue counters can be grouped as four pairs and one lone.
Pair the two leftover counters together, creating an eighth pair.
Every counter now has a partner, so the combined 16-counter group is even.

reasoning_route.action: Partition each odd group into full pairs and one lone.
reasoning_route.why_valid: Odd collections always have exactly one unmatched counter.

reasoning_route.action: Explain that the two lone counters form a new complete pair, leaving zero leftovers.
reasoning_route.why_valid: The combination preserves both counters; they can be matched with each other.

reasoning_route.action: Check eight pairs account for all 16 counters.
reasoning_route.why_valid: Three plus four existing pairs plus the new pair equals eight.

answer.check: Three plus four plus one pairs equals eight; 7+9=16 equals 2×8.

scaffolds.text: Arrange EACH original odd group into whole pairs and identify any leftover counter; do not yet describe the combined groups.

grade9v3:cognitive_demand.basis: Infer and explain the parity mechanism for a missing subgroup from a fully pairable total and a known odd subgroup; numerical subtraction is an independent check, not the explanation.

grade9v3:analysis.stable_crux_move: An unmatched counter in the known odd subgroup must meet an unmatched one from the remainder to keep the whole total pairable.
grade9v3:analysis.common_wrong_route: Simply write 18−7=11 or treat removing an odd subgroup as leaving even.

questions.stem: INVERSE explanation: one collection has 18 counters, all arranged in 9 complete pairs. A first subgroup has 7 counters (three pairs and one leftover). The remaining subgroup has 11 counters. Explain WHY the remaining subgroup must also have ONE unmatched counter, using the pair structure of the original 18 counters, not just 18−7=11.
conditions: The full collection has 18 counters and is perfectly pairable.
Seven are put into the first subgroup, leaving eleven in the second.
An odd count means one unmatched counter in a pairing.
This is an original TEST mechanism question.

answer.summary: The 7-counter subgroup has one leftover. The 18-counter total has no leftover, so the other 11-counter subgroup must also contribute one leftover to pair with it. Therefore the remaining 11 counters are odd.
reasoning: The full group of 18 has no lone counter.
The first seven have three pairs plus one lone.
For the whole collection to have no lone counter, a lone from the remaining subgroup must pair with the first group's lone.
The remaining 11 has five pairs and one lone, agreeing with the given count.

reasoning_route.action: Use the total's pairability and the first subgroup's one leftover.
reasoning_route.why_valid: The total has 9 whole pairs and the first group of 7 has 3 pairs plus one.
reasoning_route.output: total no leftover, first group one lone

reasoning_route.action: Explain why the remaining group must have a lone counter to match the first group's leftover.
reasoning_route.why_valid: A lone from the first subgroup cannot disappear; since 18 has no lone, the other subgroup must supply its partner.

reasoning_route.action: Check remaining eleven as five pairs plus one lone.

answer.check: 18−7=11=2×5+1; seven and eleven each leave a lone, and the two lone counters form one complete pair.

independent_check.statement: Verify remainder 11 and show 11=2×5+1 while 7=2×3+1; two leftovers together are paired.

difficulty.basis: Given the 18/7/11 values and the pair model, state one mechanism linking a lone from the first subgroup to the remainder; D1 band is provisional pending reviewer.

transfer.statement: The forward Core2A task combines two known odd groups and explains evenness. Here the even complete group and one odd subgroup are given, and the learner explains why the other subgroup must be odd.
transfer.invariant: Two lone counters must match to leave zero unpaired in a combined even collection.

novelty.why_new: Inverse explanation from full even group plus an odd component, rather than new odd addends or a restatement of the forward worked example. Both subgroup sizes are given, so one causal link remains.
